title: Historical introduction
paras: China, from the Shang dynasty to AD 1911

The history of China spans more than three thousand years from the Shang dynasty, which tradition placed in 1766 BC and which is now dated to around 1600 BC, and until AD 1911 it was ruled by emperors. It is usually told by dynasties, that is, by the families that held the throne, in an agricultural civilisation sustained by rice in the south and by millet and wheat in the north, so that most of the population were peasants.

Antiquity (c. 1600-221 BC). Under the Shang and the Zhou the king's power was shared with great warrior families, which ended up breaking away into rival states. Confucius lived in the last centuries of the Zhou, and in the Warring States period (5th-3rd centuries BC) those states fought one another for control of the territory.

Empire (221 BC-AD 1911). In 221 BC the Qin unified the country under an emperor, an absolute sovereign who ruled as the 'Son of Heaven', and the Han (206 BC-AD 220) made Confucianism the doctrine of the state. After centuries of division, the Tang (618-907) and the Song (960-1279) gave China its most splendid period, until it was conquered by two peoples from the north, the Mongols (1279-1368) and, after the Ming (1368-1644), the Manchus of the Qing dynasty (1644-1911). In the 19th century AD defeats by the European powers and Japan and great internal revolts weakened the Qing, until the revolution of AD 1911 overthrew the last emperor.

Republic of China (1912-1949). The Republic failed to govern the whole country, which was divided among warlords until the Nationalist Party unified it in AD 1928, and it then suffered the Japanese invasion (1937-1945) and a civil war won by the communists, so the nationalist government withdrew to Taiwan.

People's Republic of China (since AD 1949). The Communist Party proclaimed it in AD 1949 and ruled as a single party, collectivising land and industry. From the late 1970s its leaders opened the economy to the market, without giving up the party's political control.

title: Chinese society
paras: Imperial China, 221 BC-AD 1911
Emperor
'Son of Heaven'

Emperor. Confucian doctrine ordered society into four occupations, below the emperor, the 'Son of Heaven', who ruled with the imperial family and a court in which the palace eunuchs came to amass great power.
Scholars
shi

Scholars (shi). They were the men educated in the classics of Confucius. From the 7th century AD, whoever passed the imperial examinations could become a mandarin, that is, a state official, and those who passed without an office formed the local elite of each village. As preparing took years of study, only families with land could do it.
More prestige
Peasants and artisans
nong · gong

Peasants (nong) and artisans (gong). The peasants, the great majority of the population, came second because their work fed the state and paid the taxes, although many were tenants on other people's land. After them came the artisans, valued for producing useful goods.
Merchants
shang

Merchants (shang). They occupied the lowest rung, because they were accused of growing rich without producing, and the state kept them out of office. Many were richer than the scholars and bought land and education for their sons, so the pyramid measured prestige and not wealth.
Outside the scale
soldiers · Buddhist monks · base people

Outside the scale. There remained the soldiers, with little prestige among the scholars, the monks of Buddhism, which arrived from India around the 1st century AD, and of Taoism, and the base people, that is, slaves, servants, actors and acrobats. Access to exercise depended on this order, since horses, weapons and free time were in the hands of the court, the elite and the army.

title: Chinese women and exercise
paras: China, 2nd century BC-17th century AD

Chinese women lived subordinate to their father, their husband and, in widowhood, their son. Even so, throughout history it was almost always accepted that they should exercise, above all at court, so that a woman's place in Chinese sport depended on her rank more than on her sex.

In the early centuries of the Empire the swing already entered the palace for the concubines and their maids, because its name sounded like 'long life'. Between the 7th and 13th centuries AD the court formed teams of maids who learned dance, ball games and polo in a special school and performed before the emperor at the great festivals. The funerary figurines of the period, like the one in the image, show that an active woman was considered attractive.

From the 10th century AD that ideal changed. Beauty came to mean a delicate and restrained woman, who covered her face and travelled in a closed sedan chair, and foot-binding spread, beginning among the dancers of the 10th or 11th centuries AD and reaching well-to-do households, where mothers bound their daughters' feet at the age of five or six. Women's prominence in games declined from the 13th century AD, although later paintings still show ladies playing ball.

title: Traditional Chinese sport
paras: China, from Antiquity to the 19th century AD
Chinese physical culture had two faces that often complemented each other:
One sought health, longevity and harmony of the spirit,
and the other was competition, linked above all to war, the court and festivals.

The first rested on Chinese medicine, according to which qi, the vital energy, flows through the body. A person was healthy when qi circulated without blockages and yin and yang, two opposite and complementary forces, such as rest and activity, were in balance. That is why exercise had to be gentle, because excessive effort exhausted that energy, and it combined breathing, movement and calm, often imitating animals.

Nor did Chinese thought value muscular development, since Taoism sought a long life in harmony with nature and Confucianism judged a person by his virtue, so that, unlike the Greek athlete, a strong body brought no prestige.
From that first face came Hua Tuo's five animals, the gymnastics and massage of the court and the exercises of Shaolin, the basis of today's tai chi.

title: Hua Tuo and the five animals
paras: Health and longevity
China, 2nd century BC-3rd century AD

Chinese health gymnastics is called daoyin, 'guiding and stretching', and was practised to prevent old age and illness. Its oldest image is a painting on silk from a tomb at Mawangdui, sealed in 168 BC, with 44 figures in stretching and breathing postures, half of them women according to Speak (1999a).

The physician Hua Tuo, who lived between the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD, arranged those exercises into the game of the five animals, which imitates the movements of the tiger, the deer, the bear, the monkey and the bird. According to his biography, the body needed to move in order to digest food, circulate the blood and avoid illness, just as the hinge of a door that never rests does not rust.

Three of those animals already appear in the Mawangdui texts, so Hua Tuo did not invent the forms, although he gave them a coherent system. At any discomfort one of the animals had to be practised until sweating, and with that the body grew lighter and recovered its appetite.
The five animals are still practised today as part of qigong, 'work of the energy', a name that became widespread in the 20th century AD to bring together these traditional health exercises.

title: Gymnastics and massage
paras: Health and longevity
China, 7th-13th centuries AD

Chinese medicine joined gymnastics and massage because it saw them as two ways of caring for the same energy. Gymnastics moved it from within, with movement and breathing, and massage from without, by pressing on the skin, like the physician in the image, and self-massage served as a warm-up before the exercises.

In the 7th century AD both became part of the official medicine of the court, where the massage specialist also directed the exercises. The treatises of the period arranged them according to the illness they cured, so that each patient could look up his own.
Later, from the 10th century AD, simple exercises appeared that anyone could do anywhere and at any time, such as the eight brocades (ba duan jin), which are still practised today to keep healthy.

title: Bodhidharma and Shaolin
paras: China, 5th-21st centuries AD

Shaolin is a Buddhist monastery founded around AD 495 in central China, and it is regarded as the cradle of kung fu, a word that in Chinese (gongfu) means 'skill achieved through effort' and that in the 20th century AD spread in the West to name the Chinese martial arts. Tradition attributes its creation to Bodhidharma (right-hand image), an Indian monk of the late 5th century AD who is said to have taught the monks, exhausted by meditation, exercises to strengthen the body.

Buddhism forbids violence, although the monastery owned large estates that had to be protected, and its inscriptions record that in the 7th century AD its monks defended them and helped a future emperor, although at that time they fought like any other troops, without an art of their own.

The Shaolin art was born when the monks specialised, first in the staff, from the 12th century AD, and in the 17th century in unarmed combat, which joined fighting with health gymnastics and breathing and so brought together the two faces of Chinese physical culture. The legend of Bodhidharma comes from a manual of AD 1624 with a forged preface, which gave those techniques an ancient and prestigious origin (Shahar, 2008).

Today Shaolin is at once a monastery, a symbol and a business. Some 400 monks live there, about a hundred of them warrior monks, who after over a decade of training must pass an examination before the abbot in technique and in reciting the Buddhist texts. Since the cinema made it famous, schools with thousands of pupils and touring companies have grown up around it, so that its kung fu is religious practice, sport and spectacle.

Young aristocrats learned the six arts, among them archery and chariot driving, and at the ceremonies of ritual archery the king judged their virtue by how they shot rather than by whether they hit.
State offices were won through tests on the classics, without any physical test, so exercise was left to those who wanted to be soldiers.
The military examination required shooting the bow on foot and on horseback, handling the lance when mounted and proving strength, for instance by lifting the bolt of a city gate.
The body went from shaping the aristocrat to shaping the soldier, and the military degree never had the prestige of the civil one.

title: Combat sports
paras: China, from the 2nd century BC to AD 1911
Wrestling fulfilled three functions in China that coexisted for centuries: preparing the soldier, entertaining the court and amusing the people.

In the army it was training for hand-to-hand combat and a way of selecting the best soldiers. In the 17th century AD the Manchu court still considered it so important that the Kangxi emperor set up a camp to recruit and train wrestlers.

At court it soon became a spectacle. In the early centuries of the Empire it was already part of the jiaodi games ('horn games', after the horned helmets of their first wrestlers), which mixed strength, acrobatics and dance and were staged for foreign embassies to show Chinese superiority. Some emperors wrestled themselves, and winning before them could open a career, as the painting in the image suggests, with the bout surrounded by musicians and spectators.
At festivals and in the street the people went to the bouts and bet on the wrestlers, a custom that spread from the 10th century AD with the growth of the cities.

Boxing, another path. Combat with fists and feet had schools from the 2nd century BC, although its named styles took shape from the 14th century AD, when the army required it of its officers and the scholarly elite despised it.

title: Jiju
paras: Jiju was polo: two teams of riders struck a ball of wood or bone with curved-headed mallets. It probably came from Persia, although there is no firm proof, and between the 7th and 9th centuries AD it became the fashionable game of the aristocracy.

For the army it was cavalry training, and every provincial governor had his own field to prepare his riders. For the court it was a prestigious spectacle: it was played on fields a thousand paces long, with flags to count the points and a military band, and it was practised by emperors and by those who passed the examinations, who celebrated their success with a match. The mural in the upper image shows that game at full gallop, and the figurines below, which were buried with nobles, prove its prestige.

It was not only the elite riders who played. Women, the elderly and less well-off people played a quieter version on donkeys, and the donkey bones found in the tomb of a 9th-century AD lady show that these animals were bred for the game (Hu et al., 2020).
From the 10th century AD the new scholarly elite saw it as a dangerous and useless vice, and by around AD 1187 nine out of ten court officials did not even ride a horse (Liu, 1985).

title: Chuiwan, a stick-and-ball game
paras: China, 10th-17th centuries AD
The Xuande emperor playing chuiwan · China, AD 1425-1435 · Palace Museum, Beijing

Chuiwan ('striking the ball') consisted in driving a wooden ball into holes marked with flags by striking it with clubs, and each hole made in few strokes earned counters, until one player gathered ten or twenty and won the game. Unlike jiju, it had no military use, since it was an elite pastime in which prestige was won and bets were placed.

Its rules are known from the Wan jing ('Classic of the Ball'), a treatise of AD 1282. The course made use of slopes and natural obstacles, and each player used about ten clubs with bamboo shafts and wooden heads, different for each stroke, so the equipment was costly. Each hole was played from a base (ji), a square of about 30 cm facing the hole, which once drawn could not be moved, stepped on or touched. Between the base and the hole there were from about 3 m up to 50 or 60 paces, never more than a hundred, and if anyone came closer than a metre and a half to the base, his group lost.

Players were ranked in categories according to their level, with different prizes for each, and they were expected to play with calm and good manners, without losing their temper when they missed or mocking their opponent. That is why it has often been compared with golf, although nothing suggests that one derives from the other.

It began among high officials and reached the court, as the painting of the Xuande emperor playing in the palace gardens shows. From the 14th century AD it became very popular among the lower classes, and other images show children and women playing it.

title: Cuju
paras: Court
China, 4th century BC-17th century AD

Cuju or tsu-chu, from cu ('to kick') and ju ('ball'), is the oldest forerunner of football, and according to tradition it goes back to the third millennium BC. It is believed to have been a game devised to keep soldiers from suffering frostbite in their feet during winter campaigns.

Over time matches were standardised and a set of rules was laid down that turned it into a structured sport much appreciated among the Chinese elites. Matches had a head referee and an assistant, and there were official teams, the oldest known of which was called yuanshe.
There were even player transfers and skill tests to join the teams, such as making a hundred touches in a row without the ball touching the ground, and in some periods there was also women's cuju.

It was a prestigious game at court, where it was played by officials, soldiers and the sons of the rich, like those in the painting, in court robes and caps. The best players became professionals, who lived off the game and performed at festivals and in the cities.

title: Cuju and its forms
paras: China, from the 2nd century BC to the 19th century AD
There were three main forms.
With two goals. A form played by large teams, generally in the open.
With twelve semicircular goals. It was played on an enclosed field, with twelve players per team, six defenders and six forwards, and it was the most regulated form.

With a single goal. In this form, called baida, the ball had to be 'shot' through a ring placed high up. It was played between the 12th and 18th centuries AD and, allowing for the differences, resembled today's volleyball.

The ball. At first it was a ball of stuffed leather filled with hair or feathers, heavy and with little bounce. Later it was made of several stitched pieces of leather with an animal bladder inflated with air inside, which was lighter and made it possible to keep it in the air and kick it high.

title: Historical introduction
paras: Japan, from the 3rd century BC to the present

Origins (up to AD 710). Tradition places the birth of the monarchy in 660 BC, although rice farming and metal arrived from the mainland around the 3rd century BC. Between the 3rd and 6th centuries AD the kingdom of Yamato, ruled by the ancestors of the imperial family, unified much of the country, and in the 6th century AD writing and Buddhism arrived from China and Korea.

Classical period (AD 710-1185). In the 7th century AD a centralised state on the Chinese model was established, with its capital at Nara from AD 710 and at Heian, present-day Kyoto, from AD 794, where a court aristocracy ruled that took its refined games from China.

Age of the warriors (AD 1185-1603). From AD 1185 the shogun governed, a military leader who acted in the emperor's name supported by the daimyo, the lords of the land, and by a warrior class, the samurai. After a 16th century AD of civil wars, the country was unified again.

Edo period (AD 1603-1868). After defeating his rivals in AD 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu was named shogun and his family ruled from Edo, present-day Tokyo, for more than two and a half centuries of peace. The shogunate directly controlled the richest lands and the great cities and left the rest to the daimyo, whom it watched closely. To avoid foreign influence it banned Christianity and closed the country almost completely, except to the Dutch and the Chinese at Nagasaki.

Modern Japan (since AD 1868). The arrival of Commodore Perry's fleet in AD 1853 forced the country to open and hastened the Meiji Restoration of AD 1868, which returned power to the emperor, abolished the privileges of the samurai and industrialised the country, while foreign teachers introduced baseball, football and rowing. After the defeat of AD 1945, a new constitution reduced the emperor to a symbol of the state.

title: Japanese society
paras: Japan, Edo period, AD 1603-1868
Emperor
and shogun

Emperor and shogun. Authority came in theory from the emperor, who lived in Kyoto, although the shogun governed. In the Edo period the shogun controlled the court and obliged the daimyo, lords of some 260 domains, to reside in Edo one year in two and to leave their families there.
Samurai
shi

Samurai (shi). They were the hereditary warrior class, between 6 and 7 % of the population, and the only ones entitled to carry two swords. With peace they moved to the castle towns, received a stipend from their lord and went from warriors to officials.
More prestige
Peasants and artisans
nō · kō

Peasants (nō) and artisans (kō). The peasants, about 80 % of the population, came second because the taxes, which were levied on the whole village, came from their work. After them came the artisans, who lived in the towns alongside the merchants.
Merchants
shō

Merchants (shō). They occupied the lowest rung of the official order, although many grew rich and filled Edo and Osaka with kabuki theatres, teahouses and pleasure quarters, such as the Yoshiwara in Edo.
Outside the scale
monks · actors · eta

Outside the scale. There remained the monks, the actors and the artists, who could enjoy respect or fame, and at the opposite extreme the outcasts, such as the eta, who dealt with burials, executions and dead animals. Access to exercise depended on this order, since the sword and the bow were reserved for the samurai.

title: Japanese women
paras: Japan, 3rd-19th centuries AD

The position of Japanese women worsened over time. In the early centuries there were queens and empresses, such as Himiko or Suiko (AD 592-628), and with the centralised state of the 7th century AD a wife kept her own property and women received court ranks of their own, although at palace ceremonies they attended behind bamboo blinds.

In the age of the warriors, a woman of a samurai family could inherit land and was expected to show the same mettle as a man, which is why she learned to wield the naginata to defend the house. From the 14th century AD inheritance passed to a single son and she lost that right.
In the Edo period she was required to obey her father, her husband and her son, above all in samurai families, since in the towns married life was freer.

title: Japanese sport
paras: Japan, 7th-21st centuries AD
Japanese sport changed with each period and with the group that held power, so it is studied in four worlds.
The court. In the classical period the nobility played games of etiquette and beauty, such as kemari, in which elegance and form mattered more than winning.
The warriors. The bow, the sword and wrestling were the training of the samurai, and with the Tokugawa peace they became a way (-dō) of moral formation.
The city. In the Edo period merchants and artisans paid to watch spectacles, such as sumo, with idols, bets and prints of their favourite wrestlers.
Towards modern sport. With the Meiji Restoration those practices became sports with rules, grades and competition, such as judo or karate.

title: Kemari
paras: Japan, 7th-19th centuries AD

Kemari was a ball game for 6 to 12 players arranged in a circle. It is first recorded in AD 644 and is a development of the Chinese cuju or tsu-chu. The activity consists of kicking a ball to keep it from touching the ground, and each player may strike it a maximum of three times.

The ball was a hollow ball of deerskin. The players wear traditional kimonos and 'duck-bill' shoes, like the one in the image, and the correct way to strike the ball is with the body upright, moving only the legs.

The game reproduced the hierarchy of the court. In each corner of the field there was a tree, and the pine was reserved for the players of highest rank, while the colour of the clothes depended on each player's category. In AD 1208 a former emperor even granted a court rank to the ball itself.
It is a game that seeks abstraction, relaxation and the disconnection of the mind. Consecutive kicks are sometimes counted, and the oldest recorded record is 5,158 touches in AD 1683.

title: Samurai
paras: Japan, 10th-19th centuries AD

The samurai (from saburau, 'to serve') arose between the 10th and 11th centuries AD. They came above all from provincial families with land, some of them lesser branches of the nobility far from the court, who armed themselves to defend their domains and served the great lords. Their status became hereditary, and they formed the warrior class in the service of a daimyo, to whom they were bound by vassalage.
Their code of conduct, bushidō ('way of the warrior'), set out the duties of the samurai.
Elitism. It reinforced the idea that the samurai were an elite superior to the rest of the population.
Loyalty. Every samurai was obliged to give military service to his lord whenever he called on him.

Zen. Many samurai practised Zen, the branch of Buddhism that arrived from China in the 12th and 13th centuries AD, which seeks spiritual balance through meditation and self-control, and this reinforced their discipline.
Seppuku. Seppuku or harakiri was the ritual suicide the samurai performed when he failed in his task, and it was considered the greatest proof of loyalty to his lord.

With the peace of the Edo period the samurai became a bureaucratic class, far removed from their warrior function, and it was then that they set down in writing this ideal of the warrior that they no longer lived on the battlefield.

title: Samurai weapons
paras: Japan, 12th-19th centuries AD
Armour. Made of iron or lacquered leather plates laced together with cords, it could weigh around thirty kilos, and some had a mask to protect the face.

Katana. A curved, single-edged steel sword, which the samurai always carried with him as a symbol of his status. Even so, for centuries the decisive weapons on the battlefield were the bow and the spear.
Wakizashi. A short sword that the samurai carried alongside the katana. The pair of swords, called daishō ('large and small'), was the badge of his class.
Yumi. A bow of bamboo and wood, more than two metres long, with the grip set low, which gives it its characteristic asymmetric shape and made it possible to shoot from horseback.
Naginata. A long polearm ending in a curved blade, traditionally taught to the samurai and adopted by the women of warrior families as their main weapon to defend the house.
Yari. A straight-bladed spear, which with the arrival of firearms in the 16th century AD became the weapon of the foot soldiers.

title: Samurai training (archery)
paras: Japan, 12th-19th centuries AD

Kyūdō. The Japanese art of archery, literally 'way of the bow', practised with the yumi bow. It has become a ritual that seeks mastery through self-discipline, and each shot must follow a strict order. In samurai times training consisted of shooting 1,000 arrows a day, and today it is a sport practised by men and women who seek balance and spiritual relaxation.

Yabusame. Archery on horseback in which three shots were fired at three wooden targets at the gallop, with blunt-tipped arrows. Yabusame was created to improve the riding skills of the samurai. Only the most prestigious warriors were allowed to train in it.

title: Tōshiya
paras: Kyoto, AD 1606-1861

The tōshiya ('passing arrows') was an archery contest born with the Tokugawa peace, when the bow was hardly used in war any more. It was held between AD 1606 and 1861 in the gallery of the Sanjūsangendō temple in Kyoto, 120 metres long.

From one end, the archer had to shoot the arrows the whole length of the gallery without touching the roof or the pillars, so each arrow had to fly almost in a straight line. Judges from rival schools marked each hit with flags, as the painting shows, with the archers in the foreground and the target at the far end of the gallery.

The most famous test lasted 24 hours without a break. In AD 1686 an archer scored 8,133 hits, more than five a minute, and the result was recorded exactly, so the tōshiya already shows a feature of modern sport: the pursuit of the record.

title: Samurai training (combat)
paras: Japan, 16th-20th centuries AD
Kendo, literally 'way of the sword', was created for training the samurai in the use of the katana. Calm, restraint and waiting for the right moment were the skills it sought to develop.

For centuries it was practised with wooden swords, which caused serious injuries and even deaths, so the schools only performed prearranged forms (kata). In the 18th century AD some introduced the hollow sword of bamboo slats and a black outfit that protected the body from head to foot, like that of the practitioner in the image, and it became possible to strike at full contact without injury.

The sword is held with both hands, and only strikes with the upper quarter of the sword to the torso, the head, the throat or the wrists are valid. After the Meiji Restoration kendo became a path of moral formation, compulsory in schools from AD 1931.
Today it is a competitive sport with a system of ranks or dan, practised by both men and women.

title: Jūjutsu
paras: Japan, 16th-19th centuries AD

Jūjutsu (ju, 'gentle', and jutsu, 'technique') literally meant 'gentle art', and its principle was the triumph of agility over brute force. It uses the energy of the opponent's attack to defeat him through counterattacks, joint locks, strangles or holds, as in the print.

Contrary to what is often believed, it did not arise so that peasants could defeat the samurai; it was a resource of the warriors themselves when they lost their weapon on the battlefield and had to subdue an armoured enemy.

The first schools appeared in the mid-16th century AD, and in the Edo period, without wars, they adapted the techniques to an unarmoured opponent and also taught them to guards, police and ordinary people. Hundreds of schools (ryū) came to exist, each with its secret techniques, and in the 19th century AD jūjutsu had a bad name, because many masters made a living from street fights and exhibitions.
Kanō Jigorō, who took it as the basis of judo, wanted to distance himself from that bad name.

title: Sumo
paras: Japan, 8th-19th centuries AD

Sumo is Japan's national sport. The official chronicles, written in AD 720, place its origin in a legendary bout before the emperor and record other, older bouts, even between palace women, although the first reliable evidence is a court sumo held every year from AD 734, for which the provinces sent wrestlers as tribute (Guttmann & Thompson, 2001). At the same time, sumo formed part of the shrine rites to ask for good harvests, a religious origin that its ceremony still preserves.
The aim of the bouts is to throw the opponent down or push him out of the fighting ring, called the dohyō, as in the tournament in the print.

In today's professional sumo, the wrestlers (rikishi) must complete nine years of compulsory training in a stable, that is, a training centre. They are subject to a strict way of life, which includes the obligation to follow a high-fat diet to reach the average of 150 kg that each wrestler weighs.

That weight has a sporting explanation: since there are no weight classes and whoever pushes the opponent out of the ring wins, mass gives stability and drive, although the wrestlers combine it with strength, flexibility and explosiveness.

title: Sumo (II)
paras: Japan, 17th-20th centuries AD

Sumo bouts are short and intense. That is why the preparation beforehand is very important, loaded with great ceremony, which is even longer than the bout itself and serves at the same time for activation and focus.

The bout is directed by the gyōji, the referee, who wears a court costume of the Heian period, like the one in the image, and gives the start with the gunbai, a wooden war fan with which samurai generals gave orders to their troops. The wrestlers crouch face to face in the dohyō, a clay ring of about 4.5 metres covered with sand, and the fight begins when both put their fists on the ground. Whoever leaves the ring or touches the ground with anything other than the feet loses, and doubtful decisions are reviewed by judges seated around it.

The leg-raising, or shiko, is explained by tradition as a way of driving evil spirits out of the ring by hard stamping on the ground, and for the same purpose the wrestlers clap in the air or throw handfuls of salt.
However, much of that ritual was created in the Edo period to lend prestige to a paying spectacle, which is why Guttmann and Thompson (2001) present sumo as an invented tradition.

title: Judo
paras: Japan, since AD 1882

Judo (ju, 'gentle', and dō, 'way') is a martial art derived directly from jūjutsu. It was created by the master Kanō Jigorō in AD 1882 and perfected by his disciple Mifune Kyūzō, who appear together in the image.

For Kanō, judo was above all a method of all-round education, and victory was no more than a means for the physical, moral and intellectual formation of the practitioner. That is why he chose the suffix -dō, 'way', instead of -jutsu, 'technique', and based his teaching on science and rationalism, as against the secrecy with which the traditional schools guarded their techniques.

He summed up judo in two principles. The first, seiryoku zen'yō, 'maximum efficiency with minimum effort', consists of using the opponent's strength instead of opposing one's own. The second, jita kyōei, 'mutual welfare and benefit', teaches that the practitioner progresses together with the partner and not at his expense, so the opponent is a collaborator rather than an enemy.

To avoid injuries, Kanō designed grips, throws, holds and strangles of great beauty and plasticity, ordered rank with the kyu and dan grades and in AD 1926 created an official women's section at the Kodokan. His project, however, clashed with the nationalism of the time, which from the 1930s turned much of judo towards military ends.

title: Karate
paras: Okinawa and Japan, 17th-21st centuries AD

Karate (kara, 'empty', and te, 'hand') is the art of fighting without weapons, with strikes of the fist, leg, elbow and knee. Unlike judo, it was not born in the Japan of the samurai; its home was Okinawa, the main island of the kingdom of Ryūkyū, an independent state between China and Japan until the 19th century AD.

There a local fighting art, te, merged with the Chinese boxing that arrived through trade, which is why it was at first called tōde, 'Chinese hand'. Tradition says it arose because the people were forbidden to carry weapons, an explanation now considered more legendary than historical. It was taught in secret, from master to pupil, and without competition.

After the annexation of Okinawa by Japan in AD 1879, it entered the island's schools as physical education, and in AD 1922 the master Funakoshi Gichin took it to Tokyo. There it was Japanised: in the 1930s, in a time of nationalism, its name was rewritten from 'Chinese hand' to 'empty hand', and it adopted from judo the uniform, the belts and the grades (dan).
Today it is practised in two forms, kata, a sequence of movements against an imaginary opponent, and kumite, combat with a real opponent, and it made its Olympic debut at the Tokyo 2020 Games.

title: Bo-taoshi
paras: A term formed from the verb 'to bring down' (taoshi) and the word 'pole' (bō).

A team game that originated as a practical activity in Japanese military academies, possibly from the late 19th century AD. Its popularity, however, came when Japan's National Defense Academy made it a compulsory activity after the Second World War.
It is played by two teams of 150 players each, divided into 75 attackers and 75 defenders.
The aim is to bring down a pole standing upright to 30 degrees from the ground. Each team usually has a key player called the 'pole rider', who sits on top of it to keep it balanced.

Bo-taoshi serves to perfect offensive and defensive strategies and to use coordinated techniques involving a large number of participants, which is considered of great value for improving military skills.

title: Historical introduction
paras: The history of India spans almost five millennia, from the civilisation of the Indus valley, the river that gives the country its name, to independence in AD 1947. The Indian subcontinent is usually divided into three great regions, the Himalayas, the plain of the Indus and the Ganges and the Deccan plateau, surrounded by coastal plains.

Indus civilisation (c. 2600-1700 BC). The first great cities arose, whose script has still not been deciphered. Their decline, perhaps due to changes in the climate and in the course of the rivers, left the north in the hands of herding peoples.

Vedic period (c. 1400-500 BC). The Aryans, speakers of an Indo-European language, then arrived from the north-west, and their sacred texts, the Vedas, laid the foundations of Hinduism and of the caste order. Over time they settled in the Ganges valley, where the first kingdoms and new religions, such as Buddhism, arose.

Great empires (c. 320 BC-AD 500). From those kingdoms came the first empire, the Maurya, which unified almost the whole country and whose most famous emperor, Ashoka (268-233 BC), spread Buddhism across Asia. After its fall, the Gupta empire gave India its classical age, which ended with the invasions of the Huns in the 6th century AD.

Kingdoms and sultanates (AD 500-1526). Without a central power, the country split into regional kingdoms, which made it easier for Muslim conquerors to arrive from Afghanistan, and in AD 1206 they founded the Delhi sultanate and brought Islam and Persian culture to the court.

Mughal empire (AD 1526-1858). In AD 1526 Babur, a prince from Central Asia, defeated the last sultan and founded the Mughal empire, which ruled almost all of India until, in the 18th century AD, it broke up into rival kingdoms.

British rule (AD 1757-1947). That division was exploited by the East India Company, which gradually conquered the country, and after a great rebellion in AD 1857 India passed to the British Crown. The British brought cricket and hockey and despised many Indian practices, until a long nationalist movement, led by Gandhi, won independence in AD 1947, with the country divided into India and Pakistan.

title: Indian society
paras: India, from the Vedic period to the 19th century AD

Indian society was ordered in castes, groups closed by birth that fixed occupation and marriage. A late hymn of the Rigveda has the four orders (varnas) born from the body of a primordial being, Purusha, from his mouth, his arms, his thighs and his feet, as the chart shows.
Brahmins. Born from the mouth, they were the priests, in charge of sacred knowledge, the study of the Vedas and the performance of rites, and they stood at the top because of their ritual purity.
Kshatriyas. Born from the arms, they were the kings and warriors, in charge of governing and protecting, and the only ones entitled to weapons and to training in them.
Vaishyas. Born from the thighs, they devoted themselves to trade, farming and herding. Together with the Brahmins and Kshatriyas they formed the three upper orders.

Shudras. Born from the feet, they occupied the lowest rung and had to serve the upper orders. In practice society was divided into thousands of jatis, closed birth groups, whose rigid classification owes much to the British censuses of the 19th century AD (Dirks, 2001).

Outside the scale. There remained the untouchables and the forest peoples, who did work considered impure and lived outside the village. That is why access to exercise depended on caste, and training in arms was reserved for the Kshatriyas.

title: Indian women
paras: India, from the Vedic period to the 19th century AD

Indian women lived subordinate to men, and their situation worsened over time. In the Vedic period the wife took part in the rites, although from around the turn of the era treatises such as the Laws of Manu subjected her to the control of her father, her husband and, in widowhood, her son.

Marriage was arranged by families within the same caste, and among the upper castes girls were married very young. The epics also show the svayamvara, a test of strength or skill among suitors in which the bride was the prize of the contest.

Widowhood was a misfortune, and an upper-caste widow could not remarry and had to live apart. In some cases, above all in the north, sati was practised, the death of the widow on her husband's funeral pyre, which the British banned in AD 1829.

That ideal of the faithful wife (pativrata) worked, according to Chakravarti (2018), as a confinement of women, and it explains why the sources hardly mention sportswomen, except those of the court, like the lady in the image.

title: Indian sport
paras: India, from Antiquity to the 20th century AD

Indian sport was bound up with caste and religion, so each group had its own practices, and it is studied in three worlds. The epics already show it, as in the scene in the image, in which the god Krishna defeats the wrestlers of a tyrant king.
The discipline of the body. Ascetics and religious men sought through yoga health and control of body and mind as a path to spiritual liberation.
Combat. Weapons were the privilege of the Kshatriyas, while wrestling was trained in the akhara, open to high and low castes, with a way of life like that of an ascetic.
Play and festival. In the villages people played kabaddi and ran ox races at festivals, and at court chaturanga, the forerunner of chess, was born.

title: Yoga
paras: India, from Antiquity to the 20th century AD

Yoga is a set of postural and breathing exercises (āsanas) combined with meditation. Its aim is the pursuit of nirvana, a state of mental liberation in which the individual manages to free himself from worry, desire and suffering.

It has been traced back more than 5,000 years on the strength of an Indus valley seal with a seated figure, although that reading is speculative. Its classical text, the Yogasūtras, attributed to the sage Patañjali around the 3rd century AD, gathers 195 aphorisms on the techniques and theories of yoga.
As they were texts written without drawings, the yoga postures were interpreted in many different ways, which gave rise to a great number of schools, like the yogi in the image.

The yoga practised in gyms today is, to a large extent, modern. In the early 20th century AD Indian teachers such as Krishnamacharya mixed the old postures with European gymnastics and British military exercises, and created dynamic sequences of many postures, as against the fifteen described in the medieval manuals. Singleton (2010) regards it as a nationalist physical culture, later exported to the West as a practice of health and well-being.

title: Kalarippayattu
paras: India (Kerala), from the 12th century AD to the present

Kalarippayattu is a danced combat with real weapons, from the south of India, in present-day Kerala. Its name joins kalari, the earth pit that was both gymnasium and temple, and payattu, 'practice'. Many present it as the oldest martial art in Asia, although the sources only allow it to be documented with certainty from the 12th century AD.

Training had three stages. First, body-control exercises, with jumps, kicks and animal postures. Then wooden weapons, for three or four years. Finally metal weapons, from the dagger to the sword and shield, as in the image, the spear and the urumi, a flexible whip-sword worn as a belt.
At the end the marmas were studied, 107 vital points of the body that served both to attack and to heal, so the master was also a healer and treated injuries with oil massage.

After resistance by some lords of Kerala, the British banned it in the 19th century AD, and it survived only in secret within some families, until the nationalism of the 20th century AD recovered it as a symbol of local identity.

title: Wrestling (kushti)
paras: India, 12th-20th centuries AD

Kushti is the traditional wrestling of northern India and takes place in an earth pit moistened with oil, buttermilk and spices. The wrestlers wear only a small loincloth and have their bodies covered in oil or mud, like those in the image.
In the past bouts lasted until one opponent gave up. Nowadays throwing the opponent down once is enough for victory, so they usually last between 5 and 10 minutes.

Wrestlers train in gyms called akhara, run by a guru who rules their exercises, their training and their way of life, so that the wrestler is likened to an ascetic. Kings and princes kept wrestlers at their courts, because their strength symbolised the power of the ruler.

The wrestler's regimen includes a diet based on milk, butter and almonds, celibacy and long series of push-ups (dand) and squats (bethak), sometimes more than a thousand a day. That is why Alter (1992) presents it as a way of life rather than a sport.

In the 20th century AD the wrestler Gama beat the best Western wrestlers in London in AD 1910 and retired unbeaten, so Indian nationalism turned him into a symbol that an Indian body could defeat the coloniser's (Sen, 2015).

title: Strength training methods
paras: India, 19th-20th centuries AD

Gadas. Maces shaped like a 'skittle' or with a long stick ending in a sphere, ranging from a few kilos up to a hundred and made of different materials. Training consists of swinging the maces rhythmically and repeatedly around the body.

Indian maces, which the British saw in the army and in the akharas, reached Europe in the 19th century AD under the name of Indian clubs and were used in military gymnastics and school gymnastics, as in the print in the upper image. In the akhara they are also used in pairs, the jori, which in competitions reached about seventy kilos (Alter, 2005).
Club exercises · Print · 19th century AD

Mallakhamb ('the wrestler's pillar'). Gymnastic exercises on a greased wooden pole up to 3.6 metres high and 40 cm thick, like the one in the lower image. Participants must complete a routine that combines agility and physical strength. It has been traced back to the 12th century AD (Roy, 2017).

However, according to Ganneri (2013), it was created in the 19th century AD by Balambhattadada Deodhar, a wrestler from Pune under the protection of the last Maratha ruler, who after his lord's defeat by the British in AD 1818 opened akharas all over India and taught it to pupils of every caste. Today it is a competitive sport, with events on the pole and on a rope.

title: Team sports
paras: India, 19th-20th centuries AD

Yubi lakpi ('coconut snatching'). A game for seven players a side from Manipur, in north-east India, that slightly recalls rugby. The ball is a greased coconut, coated with mustard oil and water, and sometimes the players also have their bodies greased, as in the upper image. A point is scored when the coconut is carried to the rival goal.

It belonged to the Meitei, the majority people of the valley, and was part of their ritual life, since it was played at the great festivals and the coconut won was then offered to the temple (Mills, 2005).
Yubi lakpi match · Manipur, India

Kabaddi. Today it is a professional sport with two teams of seven players. On each play, a team sends a 'raider' into the opposing half to catch a rival. The raider cannot breathe, so he must chant 'kabaddi' throughout the play, while the rivals form a human chain to try to tackle him, as in the lower image. Although tradition credits it with thousands of years, its first rules were fixed in the 1920s.

It was played by children and young people in the villages, with different names and rules in each region, until middle-class nationalist groups codified it and displayed it at the 1936 Berlin Games as a national sport (Alter, 2000). Today it is played on a court of about 13 × 10 metres and each raid lasts 30 seconds.

title: Ox races
paras: India, rural tradition

For farming families, ox races are a matter of prestige. The animals are raised and cared for all year round with a special diet, oil massages and rest, and they arrive at the race decorated with bells and ribbons. The winner receives prizes in cash, trophies or valuables, and a champion ox later sells for a much higher price, so the race proves the family's skill as breeders and increases its wealth.
Bailgada sharyat · Maharashtra, India

Bailgada sharyat (Maharashtra). Bullock-cart races in rural areas, during the village fairs (jatras), also called shankarpat. They are run in the dry season, and where space is short the race is against the clock, so the winner is whoever takes least time.
Kambala · Karnataka, India

Kambala (Karnataka). A buffalo race on a mud track on the coast, between November and March. It used to be run on a single track, the ontikare, and today on two parallel tracks of about 130 metres, with classes according to the tool the rider carries, such as a plough, a rope or a board.
Maramadi · Kerala, India

Maramadi (Kerala). An ox race in flooded paddy fields, similar to the kambala, held after the harvest. The runner goes barefoot, holding on to the yoke, before a crowd that cheers from the banks, as in the image. In AD 2014 the Supreme Court banned these races for animal cruelty, and several states later authorised them with laws of their own.

title: Chaturanga
paras: India and Persia, 6th-7th centuries AD

Chaturanga is a board game that is the direct forerunner of chess. Its name combines chatur ('four') and anga ('limbs'), because it reproduced the four divisions of the army of India, that is, infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots.

The pieces were the pawns, the horses, the elephants (the bishops), the chariots (the rooks) and the king, as on the board in the image. Later a version for four players with dice was also played, although Murray (1913) considers the two-player game to be the original.

The rules are not known exactly, but according to later Persian sources there were two ways of winning: 'stifling the king', that is, checkmating him as in modern chess, and 'stripping the king', that is, capturing all the pieces except the monarch.

From India it passed to Persia in the 6th century AD under the name chatrang, and after the Arab conquest the Muslims carried it across the Mediterranean to al-Andalus, in the Iberian Peninsula, from where it spread through Europe. That is why words such as 'check', from the Persian shāh, 'king', and 'mate', from shāh māt, 'the king is helpless', still keep their Persian origin.
